documentation:
## View-Based Ocean

### What it does

This graph creates an ocean mesh that is fit to the camera view.  It has more polygons closer to the camera, and less at the horizon.

### Inputs and outputs

The input for this graph is a Maya camera.  
**Please note:**  this is an external connection and is ***not*** connected by default.  There are instructions in the graph file on how to make this connection, as well as the following MEL script that will connect the Maya perspective camera to the correct input on the Bifrost graph.

```
connectAttr -f perspShape.worldMatrix[0] viewBasedOceanShape.camera_transform
```

### How it works

- A `create_spectral_waves` compound is used to generate the base ocean surface, then passed to a `simulate_foam` compound to simulate a dynamic foam.

- These are passed into a compound (`compute_if_time_changes`) which will use a feedback cache for the ocean surface and the foam if the time hasn't changed.  Enabling *always_compute* on this compound will make the ocean surface and foam reevaluate for editing purposes, but when ticked off (It's on by default) this will speed up the simulation by using cached settings for the ocean and foam.

- Everything is then passed to the `displace_ocean_geometry` compound.  This creates the view-based mesh and applies the input foam and wave data to that mesh.

_notes.text:
# View-based Ocean Mesh

This graph creates an ocean using a mesh that is fit to the camera view, with more resolution near the view point and less at the horizon. One must attach the *camera_transform* to the graph input and then connect the Maya perspective camera matrix to the this input, for example the following MEL does this:
```
connectAttr -f perspShape.worldMatrix[0] viewBasedOceanShape.camera_transform
```

Once the camera is connected to the graph input the graph will only evaluate when the connected camera changes, for example while tumbling the view. In order to avoid excessive recompute of the ocean this graph uses feedback port caches of previous states and checks if properties have been changed. When tumbling the view it then only recomputes the new camera based geometry, not the spectral wave and foam simulation. When editing properties on ***create_spectral_waves***, or simulate_foam one may wish to temporarily enable *always_compute* on ***compute_if_time_changes*** in order to see realtime feedback in the viewport. 

The node ***displace_ocean_geometry*** has properties that should be set to match those on the camera (*width, height, angle_of_view, far_clip*) The angle_of_view should typically bit a bit larger than the camera value as the mesh may displace sideways a bit. 

Before rendering one may wish to increase the *resolution_scale* to a value like 2 or more. (This would be roughly 4 poly per pixel). This may need to be relatively high to sufficiently sample along the horizon. This may make interactive tumbling in the viewport slow.

# Displace the Ocean

***displace_ocean_geometry*** creates a mesh and applies the input wave and foam arrays to this mesh.

* If *use_view_based_geo* is enabled the mesh is created in camera space and projected onto the ground, creating a wedge shaped mesh that matches the viewing frustum. If disabled it creates a simple plane mesh that fits the bounds of the base spectral wave simulation. 

* *camera_transform*:
For the view_based mesh this should be connected to the Maya camera worldMatrix[0]

* *width*, *height*, *angle_of_view*, *far_clip*:
These should be set to match the values on the Maya camera, although angle_of_view should be a bit larger to accomodate the horizontal displacement from wave peaking, otherwise one may see gaps at the image borders.

* *resolution_scale*:
This is initially set to a low value so that tumbing the view is not too slow. One could lower this further for better interactivity, but then increase to a value like 2 or more before rendering to better resolve waves near the horizon. In general it is defined relative to pixels where 1.0 would be roughly one poly per pixel.

* *exponent*: This can be used to bias the triangles toward the horizon, which typically needs more triangles per pixel then the foreground. A value of 1.0 represents no bias with higher values shifting polygons towards the horizon. The effect of this bias transitions to zero when looking straight down.

* *planet_radius*: This allows the ocean to curve away near the horizon modeling the curvature of the earth. Smaller values will have it curve away more.

* *offset_backwards*: This move the camera projection backwards a little before creating the geometry. It helps deal with slop at the edges and places where upward displacment at the bottom of the frame might cause a gap.

"compute_if_time_changes" will use feedback caches of the wave and foam if time hasn't changed. Currently it doesn't check if the properties on the spectral wave and foam have changed, so when editing one can temporarily enable always_compute so the viewport updates when editing wave and foam properties.
This is the mesh used when use_view_based_geo is OFF.
It may help on the camera to enable DisplaceResolution and DisplaceGateMask

**Note:**  This is an external input to the graph and will not be connected on load. 

Attach the *camera_transform* to the graph input and then connect the Maya perspective camera matrix to the this input, for example the following MEL does this:
```
connectAttr -f perspShape.worldMatrix[0] viewBasedOceanShape.camera_transform
This simply uses the previous output mesh if the simulation and view have not changed.
Apply foam and displacement to the geometry
Create a mesh based on the camera view

# ***translate_along_view***
Simply shift the camera backwards by the distance value, to help avoid gaps at the bottom of the frame.

# ***setup_camera_viewplane_mesh***
Create a plane that exactly fits to the camera viewplane. If the resolution scale is 1.0 then there would be a poly for each pixel.

# ***project_viewplane_to_ground***
Project that viewplane mesh along the view direction onto the ground (Y=0). The face count stays the same but in some places like the horizon some faces may flatten out on top of each other and have zero area. The view faces that would project to sky end up along the horizon line. It might be helpful to have a pass to get rid of these (zero area) polygons.

# ***compute_plane_if_changed***
Only recompute the camera mesh if the view or properties change

# ***project_to_ground***
project the viewspace plane onto the ground(Y=0)

# ***bias_distance***
This uses the exponent to shift polygons towards the horizon to better resolve waves along the horizon.

# ***planet_curvature***
Project downward onto a sphere with the defined radius.
reduce the effect of the exponent as the view looks down or up

This method locks the near clip boundary and then shifts out towards the far clip boundary, so the triangles stay in the defined view but bias towards the horizon (based on the exponent values). Exponent of 1 is no bias.

This uses feedback ports to cache previous versions of properties and compare with these to determine if anything has changed.

To simplify things the propertes are collected into a float array so we just need one feedback port.

"*using_cached*" is set inside ***compute_if_time_changes***.

This lets us know if the simulation has changed and we need to update the displacement.
This uses a cached object (*prev_object* feedback) unless time has changed, *always_compute* is on or the *prev_object* is empty (typically on the first evaluation)
This is a simple node that compares the last time evaluation and outputs if it has changed.

_notes.text: The ***set_using_cached*** is a property to flag whether this object is a new update or the same from the previous frame. If it is new the meshing later checks this property and only reapplies the displacement if needed.
```
